note: Traced episodes per locality, drawn from the the traced activity. Each entry states what the reporting shows - announced, reported or assessed - never more. Kinds follow the four actor layers, plus 'context' for conflict events that belong to no layer.

events.text: Shop owners began repairing their stores the morning after the ceasefire took effect, working amid explicit unexploded-ordnance warnings.
The Council for the South launched the response's first large rubble-clearance tender, with bids opening in January.
Roughly 5,000 business owners staged the first major protest against the slowness of both official and parallel compensation.

The Public Works Ministry's 'Reconnecting Lebanon' campaign reported road clearance and access restoration across Nabatieh and surrounding towns, partly with the army - officially reported, without published quantities.

A citywide cleanup campaign joined ambulance crews, Civil Defense, scouts, municipal workers and residents; days earlier, ambulance volunteers had cleared the central mosque for Ashura on two days' notice.
A returning family began clearing its butcher shop, with reported losses of about US$120,000 - self-financed recovery from the first days after the ceasefire.
The village financed collective solutions: prefabricated homes and a rebuilt husseiniya - recovery paid for from communal resources, not any public programme.
The locally financed Aitaroun Recovery Project bought equipment and supported returns - about 200 families returned against a 500-family target.
The UNDP–CNRS-L assessment traced 1,658 completely destroyed buildings - the worst cadaster south of the Litani, hit again after rebuilding attempts.
ISF patrols halted and fined self-financed rebuilding pending permits; work resumed after public controversy - regulation without a functioning state alternative.
969 completely destroyed buildings traced in the UNDP–CNRS-L assessment - among the worst cadasters, levelled in both wars.
ISF patrols halted and fined self-financed rebuilding pending permits, before public controversy let work resume.
Participatory workshops traced return obstacles village by village, converting testimony into planning material.
ISF patrols halted and fined self-financed rebuilding pending permits - one of three border villages where recovery was briefly criminalised.
Reporting characterised parallel-track payments to residents (February 2025) - self-reported figures, treated as unaudited.
824 completely destroyed buildings traced in the UNDP–CNRS-L assessment of the zone south of the Litani.
Mercy Corps' radar model assessed damage across 34,490 buildings in the district - one of the four non-additive damage tracks.
CDR published procurement package #1082 - supervision of road clearing and restoration in Marjeyoun, Sour and Bint Jbeil; still under evaluation at the 17 July portal check.
1,076 completely destroyed buildings traced in the UNDP–CNRS-L assessment.
Covered by CDR procurement package #1082 (road-clearing and restoration supervision with Sour and Bint Jbeil) - published, extended, and unawarded at the 17 July portal check.
Volunteer convoys from Saida arrived to help clear debris - solidarity moving along social networks, not programme logistics.
A displacement order covered all of Tyre and its Palestinian camps - de-escalation without safety.
Covered by CDR procurement package #1082 for road-clearing supervision; no award displayed at the 17 July portal check.
Volunteer convoys left Saida for Sour and Nabatieh in the ceasefire's first weeks.
A solidarity association ran a school shelter hosting about 650 families through the March displacement wave, then pivoted its volunteers to cleanup as returns began.
Offre Joie volunteers cleared 600 truckloads of debris from Karantina in eight days; the group later restored 20 buildings on Mamoun Street in Basta.
The ten-day municipal survey traced 16,000 damaged housing units in Baabda district - 63% reported completely damaged - the response's fastest damage assessments.
Cabinet assigned the southern-suburbs rubble clearance to the Union of Municipalities, which opened tenders and worked through the al-Bunyan contractor, with debris routed toward Costa Brava.
The Dahieh municipal union continued supervising rubble operations with reported sorting arrangements - while the South waited.
The UNDP–CNRS-L assessment traced 648,942 m³ of debris across Beirut–Mount Lebanon - 93% of it in Baabda district, the Dahieh belt hit in both wars.
Part of the war rubble was transferred to the landfill's third cell for support and expansion use - the official disposal interface for the southern-suburbs clearance.
UNIFIL cleared debris and reopened streets after the withdrawal from the town.
The South Lebanon Water Establishment patched the local network - emergency repair through existing chains, not programme works.
EDL restored electricity supply working with the municipality - small, local, budget-funded repair outside any published contract.
The municipality publicly reported rubble clearance - one of sixteen-plus localities lifting debris; quantities, destinations and completion not confirmable.
The municipality publicly reported rubble clearance - traced as reported; quantities cannot be confirmed.

Named in OCHA-coordinated humanitarian reporting as a locality of traced response activity.
Fell under the Higher Relief Commission's jurisdiction for damage claims and shelter coordination, alongside Mount Lebanon, Dahieh and the North.
